draft.title: Force between parallel wires
card: A current makes a magnetic field around its wire. A second wire nearby sits in that field, so it feels a force. By the same reasoning, the first wire feels a force from the second.
two parallel wires with currents in the same direction attract each other.
two parallel wires with currents in opposite directions repel each other.

The force on each wire per metre of length is F/L = μ₀I₁I₂ ÷ 2πr. Here I₁ and I₂ are the currents, r is the distance between the wires and μ₀ is a constant. The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
draft.remember: Same direction attracts, opposite repels. Force per metre grows with the currents and falls with distance.

a.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. What happens between the wires?
opts: They exert no force on each other
Only the wire with the larger current feels a force
a.why: Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other, so each feels a force. When the currents run the same way, the forces pull the wires together. The larger current does not change this: both wires feel equal forces.
a.clue: Each wire is in the field of the other, and the forces are equal.

b.q: Two parallel wires are 0.10 m apart. Wire 1 carries 4.0 A and wire 2 carries 6.0 A. The distance is then doubled. What happens to the force per metre on wire 1?
b.why: The force per metre is μ₀I₁I₂ ÷ 2πr, so it is inversely proportional to r. Doubling r halves the force. It does not quarter, because r is not squared in this formula.
b.clue: Look at how r appears in the formula.
